screenings.title: The Red Light Bandit
screenings.description: Described by Sganzerla—21 years old when he directed his wild-eyed feature debut—as a “Western about the Third World,” The Red Light Bandit drew inspiration from the exploits of João Acácio Pereira da Costa, a recently arrested career criminal who’d acquired the status of folk hero, and, in its rough-edged style and vigorous montage, from the recent output of Jean-Luc Godard. A descent into the mean streets of São Paulo’s Boca do Lixo (Mouth of Garbage) neighborhood, Sganzerla’s brash, confrontational film is one of the key works of Brazil’s Cinema Marginal movement, per its creator: “Dirty and poetic, impure and pretentious… [speaking] of politics or of banditry without aesthetic respect, to the point of adopting an obscene liberty.”

screenings.title: The Hole [Newly Struck 35mm Print]
screenings.description: It’s the close of the millennium and Taipei has emptied out with the onset of a mysterious virus, but The Man Upstairs (Lee Kang-sheng) and The Woman Downstairs (Yang Kuei-mei) lag behind among the ruins, where it doesn’t seem like there’s really much world to end, but maybe a last chance at communication through a breach between their apartments that slowly widens through Tsai’s downbeat, glum-funny dystopian masterpiece. Tsai's beloved film returns to Metrograph for a weeklong run on a newly struck 35mm print, approved by Tsai himself.

screenings.title: El Topo
screenings.description: Chilean-born mime-turned-filmmaker Jodorowsky plays the title role in this acid Western staple of the midnight movies, strapping on the six-shooter as a lone gunfighter—his name means “The Mole” in Spanish—traveling across a psychedelic desert landscape on a quest to vanquish increasingly unusual villains while simultaneously confronting his own spiritual anguish and existential dread. A mind-melting trip through the doors of perception that counted John Lennon among its many acolytes, made up of “a phantasmagoric Mexican landscape laden with dead bunnies and burros, snarling hippie chicks, pregnant silences, buckets of blood, and guru-gunslingers.”—Manohla Dargis, The New York Times

screenings.title: L'Argent
screenings.description: “In L’Argent I sense an unconditional surrender to despair and disgust. One can hardly argue that contemporary humanity does not deserve its full quotient of despair and disgust. And it is not even a matter of this social system or that. The rottenness seems to have plunged very deeply into the universal psyche. The artist, however is still obligated to search for order amid the chaos, for beauty amid the ugliness, for truth amid the falsehoods, and, above all, for hope amid the despair… That a filmmaker can lift us to these levels of contemplation and speculation is proof enough of that filmmaker’s greatness” —Andrew Sarris

screenings.title: Rambling Rose
screenings.description: Acclaimed novelist and screenwriter Calder Willingham adapted his own 1972 novel of the same name scripting Coolidge’s tender, deeply humane Great Depression-set drama, starring Dern as Rose, a teenager rescued from a life of prostitution after being taken in as a domestic by an eccentric Georgia family, her sexual precocity soon making her a destabilizing force in the household, comprised of father Robert Duvall, mother Diane Ladd, and son Lukas Haas. Dern and Ladd would become the first real-life mother-daughter duo to be nominated for acting Academy Awards in the same year for their work in Rambling Rose, which Roger Ebert raved “contains some of the best performances of the year, especially in the ensemble acting of the four main characters.”

screenings.title: The Eight Diagram Pole Fighter
screenings.description: Made as the declining Shaw Brothers Studio entered its twilight years, Lau’s Eight Diagram Pole Fighter, inspired by Song dynasty folklore, has all the radiant beauty of a spectacular sunset, a showcase for all that the Shaw machine, at the height of its fine-tuned powers, did best. Six of his seven brothers and his general father slaughtered in an ambush by Khitan barbarians, Yang Wu-lang (Gordon Liu) finds asylum at a Buddhist monastery in Mount Wutai, where he practices and develops the eponymous technique, and learns to abjure violence—though his vows of pacifism will be sorely tested when his family’s butchers resurface. “One of the most impressive of [Lau’s] last Shaw works… A somber dissection of the revenge motif… Lau’s sympathy seems largely with the monks who insist, in film after film, that revenge debases the martial arts.” —David Bordwell, Planet Hong Kong

screenings.description: It’s the close of the millennium and Taipei has emptied out with the onset of a mysterious virus, but The Man Upstairs (Lee Kang-sheng) and The Woman Downstairs (Yang Kuei-mei) lag behind among the ruins, where it doesn’t seem like there’s really much world to end, but maybe a last chance at communication through a breach between their apartments that slowly widens through Tsai’s downbeat, glum-funny dystopian masterpiece. screenings.title: The Limits of Control
screenings.description: Isaach De Bankolé is a mysterious operative in Spain on an equally obscure mission, making his way through a string of cryptic meetings en route to an appointment at a fortress-like compound overseen by a sinister Bill Murray in Jarmusch’s espionage thriller, inspired by both Spaghetti Westerns and the skeletal prose of Donald Westlake’s Parker novels, written under the pseudonym Richard Stark. Of his collaboration with improviser par excellence Doyle, Jarmusch reported: “Chris is, for me, like a river full of fish—ideas swimming past continually. And you can fish out however many or however few you want, and Chris is there to realize them… He’s also wild… Somebody said that Keith Richards met Chris and said, ‘Well, Chris Doyle is the Keith Richards of cinematographers.’”

screenings.title: Darkest Hour
screenings.description: Wright’s vital, stirring period piece biopic earned Gary Oldman a Best Actor statuette at the Academy Awards for his transformation into Sir Winston Churchill, seen here in the early days of his first stint as Prime Minister, faced with the battlefield catastrophes of Dunkirk and Calais and a War Cabinet pleading for negotiations with Hitler’s Germany. “Oldman is terrific as Churchill, conveying the babyishness of his oddly unlined face in repose, the slyness and manipulative good humour, and a weird deadness when he is overtaken with depression… [He] carries off a tremendous performance here, and it’s impossible not to enjoy it. It’s as if his establishment panjandrum George Smiley was suddenly infused with the spirit of Sid Vicious.” —The Guardian

screenings.title: State of Grace
screenings.description: “His technique was almost invisible—you couldn’t even figure out if there was one… He understood everything about Jackie, how he’d behave and speak and move.” So said director Joanou of Gary Oldman’s loose-cannon performance in State of Grace, the actor’s US breakthrough, an inspired neo-noir that follows Terry Noonan (Sean Penn) on his return to Irish American Hell’s Kitchen after a long absence—unbeknownst to friends and neighbors now an undercover cop trying to take down a criminal organization whose members include Oldman’s Jackie Flannery and his elder brother, Frank (Ed Harris). Fervent admirers of Oldman’s work here include critic Roger Ebert, who praised “the twisted vision of [his] character, who lives in a world of evil and betrayal and has somehow thought himself around to the notion that he is doing the right thing,” and Leonardo DiCaprio, who stated that Oldman’s Jackie “influenced an entire generation of actors.”

screenings.title: Collateral
screenings.description: Los Angeles cabbie Max Durocher (Jamie Foxx) is in for the toughest fare of his working life when he picks up one Vincent (Tom Cruise, natty in charcoal gray sharkskin suit), a jazz enthusiast and professional hitman who quite firmly insists that his driver accompany him on his evening’s rounds, leaving a trail of bodies in his wake. Shooting LA exteriors after dark with a then-state-of-the-art Sony F-900 digital camera, Mann gave his film a wholly distinctive texture—combining expressionistic smear with a new ability to pick up detail that would be lost on celluloid—and initiated a quiet revolution in low-light cinematography. A drum-tight character-based thriller, and the only film in which you can see Tom Cruise saying: “Yo, homie… Is that my briefcase?”

screenings.title: One Hundred and One Dalmatians
screenings.director: Clyde Geronimi, Hamilton Luske, Wolfgang Reitherman
screenings.description: Based on a children’s novel of the same name by Dodie Smith, animated musical One Hundred and One Dalmatians gave the Walt Disney pantheon one of its greatest villains in the person of vindictive and indefatigable heiress Cruella de Vil (voiced by Betty Lou Gerson), whose monomaniacal obsession with getting herself a fur coat made out of dalmatian pelts is opposed by a young London couple, their dogs, Pongo and Perdita, and Pongo and Perdita’s vast litter of puppies. A brisk, clever, and sometimes quite camp film fable.

screenings.title: The Triplets of Belleville
screenings.description: This animated film follows elderly Frenchwoman Madame Souza as she becomes involved in international intrigue when her grandson, Champion, a professional cyclist, is kidnapped and taken abroad. Joined by her faithful dog, Bruno, Souza embarks on a journey to find Champion, and stumbles across unlikely allies in the form of three sisters who are veterans of the vaudeville stage. Tracking down Champion's criminal captors, the quartet of old women use their wits to try and win the day.

screenings.title: Solaris preceded by The Working End
screenings.description: “This July, the New Humans screening series concludes with Solaris (1972), preceded by Kristin Walsh’s The Working End (2025), presented by Walsh herself. Where Solaris explores the invisible psychological forces operating beneath the surface of our perception of reality, Walsh’s abstract metallic structures make visible the usually hidden systems of labor and infrastructure that shape city life. It is in this shared interest in the invisible made visible—alongside an attention to liminality and pacing that creates uncanny moments of tension—that Tarkovsky and Walsh meet. See Walsh’s work, Engine no. 15 , 2025, on view now at the New Museum.” —Thalia Stefaniuk, series co-curator and New Museum Curatorial Assistant

screenings.title: My Little Loves
screenings.description: Coming-of-age, Eustache-style: the director followed up The Mother and the Whore with an intimate drama based on his childhood, about a boy’s awkward, provincial adolescence in the south of France. This unsentimental, elegantly somber, visually driven film about sexual self-discovery and the passage of time was gorgeously photographed by the legendary Nestor Almendros. Eustache’s only other feature-length narrative film other than The Mother and the Whore, it owns a rightful place next to that film as a true masterpiece.

screenings.title: Basic Instinct
screenings.description: The film that made a star of Sharon Stone, seen to good effect in Verhoeven’s previous Carolco production, Total Recall, and that also provided the studio a succès de scandale windfall. Perfectly poised as she negotiates her way through the most infamous police station interrogation scene in cinema, Stone’s pulp novelist-and-suspected ice pick murderess Catherine Trammell is a blonde ice queen à la Hitchcock who begins to melt in the arms of besotted SFPD Detective Nick Curran (Michael Douglas)—or does she only appear to? A work of carnivorous carnality that moves with prowling panther sleekness, its career-best Jerry Goldsmith score adding immeasurably to the undercurrent of imminent danger.

screenings.description: Described by Sganzerla—21 years old when he directed his wild-eyed feature debut—as a “Western about the Third World,” The Red Light Bandit drew inspiration from the exploits of João Acácio Pereira da Costa, a recently arrested career criminal who’d acquired the status of folk hero, and, in its rough-edged style and vigorous montage, from the recent output of Jean-Luc Godard. screenings.title: Before Sunrise
screenings.description: Linklater’s ongoing, decades-spanning story of a love affair through its many ups and downs begins here, with a chance encounter on a train between Ethan Hawke and Julie Delpy, the American Jesse and the French Céline, who together will pass a day and night in Vienna full of spirited, sparkling conversation and a slowly dawning attraction, all depicted with an ambling, uninflected naturalism. A wistful, winning, and quietly impassioned portrait of young love as it begins to bloom.

screenings.title: The Bakery Girl of Monceau + Suzanne's Career
screenings.description: Though rightfully an international arthouse phenomenon, Rohmer’s Moral Tales are remarkable in just how little they scream for attention, notable for their modesty of scale and their dedication to delicate observation rather than anything resembling firebrand provocation. The first two entries in the series are perfect instances of this: in The Bakery Girl of Monceau, a law student (a young Barbet Schroeder) flirts brazenly with the title character while brooding over his romantic failure with another girl; in Suzanne’s Career, in which two young men, a woman-shy introvert and a self-styled Don Juan, get mixed up with—and, in their individual ways, misuse—independent minded Catherine Sée, only to find their egos far more fragile than hers. Not exactly “high concept” stuff on the page, but on the screen… an abundance.

screenings.title: Do You Love Me
screenings.description: A cinematic paean to Beirut and a journey into the collective audiovisual memory of Lebanon and its people, making use of film and television clips, home movies, and photographs drawn from private and public archives, materials spanning some 70 years of turbulent history. (Among the film’s parade of faces is that of director Jocelyne Saab, subject of a concurrent Metrograph series, visiting the wreckage of her former home, reduced to rubble in a 1982 Israeli air strike.) The glorious product of reclamation and meticulous research, and an urgent dispatch from an embattled nation, Do You Love Me proffers a people’s history that eschews linear chronology to offer instead a rich rhyming network of generation-crossing associations. A film of intimacy and alienation, of destruction and renewal, of grief and resilience.

screenings.title: Bride of the Earth
screenings.description: Güney, a stubbornly individualistic, rabble-rousing talent whose cinema stirred together Kurdish/Turkish folklore and aspects of the Western into a potent and highly politicized compound, took on the lead role in this lyrical yet naturalistic breakthrough work, strikingly lensed in black-and-white widescreen, about an impoverished Anatolian villager, Seyyit, who swears revenge upon learning that a wealthy landowner has been pitching woo to his lover (Nebahat Çehre) with the intention of taking her as his wife. An ideal introduction to a larger-than-life figure described by J. Hoberman as “something like Clint Eastwood, James Dean, and Che Guevara combined,” and affectionately nicknamed “the Ugly King” by his adoring public.

screenings.title: The Hole [Newly Struck 35mm Print]
screenings.description: It’s the close of the millennium and Taipei has emptied out with the onset of a mysterious virus, but The Man Upstairs (Lee Kang-sheng) and The Woman Downstairs (Yang Kuei-mei) lag behind among the ruins, where it doesn’t seem like there’s really much world to end, but maybe a last chance at communication through a breach between their apartments that slowly widens through Tsai’s downbeat, glum-funny dystopian masterpiece. Tsai's beloved film returns to Metrograph for a weeklong run on a newly struck 35mm print, approved by Tsai himself.

screenings.title: Happy Together
screenings.description: Hong Kong cinema superstars Tony Leung and Leslie Cheung play a pair of lovers living out the waning days of their relationship as expatriates in Buenos Aires. Lusty tango bars, the salsa music of the La Boca sidewalks, and a hypnotic visit to the nearby Iguazu Falls give further dimension to the tensions growing between the two. Winner of the Best Director prize at the 1997 Cannes Film Festival, Wong’s Happy Together is a stunning display of filmmaking style and a touching story of love on the brink of dissolution.

screenings.title: Bouchra
screenings.description: Multihyphenate artists Barki and Bennani’s playful animation/live-action hybrid film à clef offers up a delightfully idiosyncratic look at the travails of the queer expat artist. The title character here is imagined as an anthropomorphic jackal inhabiting a New York City filled with other like critters, a young filmmaker simultaneously dealing with creative crises, her rocky relationship with her mother back in Casablanca, and the pleasures and perils of sex in the city. Drawing on real phone calls and myriad other correspondences, with voice talent courtesy of the directing duo’s friends and family members, this lay-it-on-the-line autofiction is at once startlingly light on its feet and densely layered with insight, not least into the feelings that come of shakily straddling two cultures while belonging fully to neither.

screenings.title: Take Care of My Cat
screenings.description: Returning to cinemas this year, celebrating its 25th anniversary re-release, the debut feature from Jeong, one of a handful of female directors to break into the South Korean film industry, focuses on five young women, recent high school graduates living in the industrial port city of Incheon and facing a precarious future together, in addition to having to handle the practical exigencies of caring for the feline that they’ve communally adopted. Bae Doona, whose Tae-hee makes ends meet with shifts at her family’s sauna and occasional work as a typist for a cerebral palsy-afflicted poet, anchors an exceedingly fine ensemble cast in Jeong’s moving drama of fraying friendships and economic uncertainty, also one of the first films to acknowledge the increasingly central role of text messaging in 21st-century communication and find a way to integrate this new, faceless form of “keeping in touch” into a filmed narrative.

screenings.title: Jacob's Ladder
screenings.description: Having proven himself a reliable hitmaker through the 1980s with Flashdance, 9½ Weeks, and Fatal Attraction, Lyne took an excursion into troubling new territory with this headlong plunge into the damaged psyche of Vietnam veteran Jacob Singer (Tim Robbins) who, haunted by his wartime experience and the death of a son, finds his drab daily life in c. 1975 New York City increasingly infringed on by nightmarish hallucinations—disturbing visions that suggest something more than run-of-the-mill PTSD. A nerve-fraying, phantasmagoric, wholly immersive waking nightmare that dangles its protagonist—and we, the audience—over a yawning abyss of horror. “Both a highly effective stream-of-consciousness puzzle thriller offering the viewer not one but many ‘solutions’ and an emotionally persuasive statement about the plight of many American vets.” —Jonathan Rosenbaum, Chicago Reader

screenings.title: Fallen Angels
screenings.description: Part hard-boiled crime thriller and part soft, featherweight giddiness, Fallen Angels was first conceived as a segment of Wong’s Chungking Express, then developed into a darker companion piece to his glistening pop-romantic masterpiece, the story of a hitman (Leon Lai) looking to hang up his gun, the business partner (Michelle Reis) who quietly lusts after him, and a mute troublemaker (Takeshi Kaneshiro) running amok in Hong Kong. Christopher Doyle’s cinematography has never been more woozily, blearily beautiful, nor has the Fragrant Harbor ever been put on screen with such transfixing nocturnal glamor.

screenings.title: In the Mood for Love
screenings.description: Wong’s arthouse smash is the very simple tale of two people in early ’60s Hong Kong, Mr. Chow (Tony Leung Chiu-wai) and Mrs. Chen (Maggie Cheung), drawn to one another by the discovery that their spouses are getting together on the side. A little story, full of little details, all surrounding a love affair that isn’t really a love affair—but throbbing with huge, aching emotions that it can barely contain. It might just break your heart.

screenings.title: Boyfriends and Girlfriends
screenings.description: Rohmer uses the amorous misadventures of two girlfriends in the Paris suburbs to test the old proverb “les amis de mes amis sont mes amis” (“the friends of my friends are my friends”) in the final episode of his “Comedies and Proverbs” series. Taking an identifiable stab at a yuppie(ish) set, Rohmer’s witty Shakespearean roundelay involves the buttoned-up Blanche (Emmanuelle Chaulet, in a superb debut) and the free-spirited Lea (Sophie Renoir), and their current amours. The pair are tempted by each other’s love interests, testing both their friendship and their understanding of matters of the heart. A Metrograph Pictures release.

screenings.title: Rebecca
screenings.description: “Last night I dreamt I went to Manderlay again…” Hitchcock was still a newly arrived UK import when this gothic thriller/romance, based on the novel of the same title by Daphne du Maurier, took Outstanding Production (later “Best Picture”) honors at the Academy Awards. Joan Fontaine stars as a terribly self-conscious young woman, never identified by name, who becomes enamored with a saturnine, aristocratic widower, Maxim de Winter (Laurence Olivier, fresh from Wuthering Heights)—and, once she’s been taken as his bride, obsessed with his late wife’s phantom presence in their home on the Cornwall coast. A marvel of directorial assurance that turns the screws with poise and panache.

screenings.title: State of Grace
screenings.description: “His technique was almost invisible—you couldn’t even figure out if there was one… He understood everything about Jackie, how he’d behave and speak and move.” So said director Joanou of Gary Oldman’s loose-cannon performance in State of Grace, the actor’s US breakthrough, an inspired neo-noir that follows Terry Noonan (Sean Penn) on his return to Irish American Hell’s Kitchen after a long absence—unbeknownst to friends and neighbors now an undercover cop trying to take down a criminal organization whose members include Oldman’s Jackie Flannery and his elder brother, Frank (Ed Harris). screenings.title: The Night is Short, Walk on Girl
screenings.description: A surreal nocturnal animated odyssey from Yuasa, the mad genius behind Mind Game, rendered in a frenetic, galaxy-brained, endlessly morphing style. The Night is Short, Walk on Girl follows a mysterious high schooler known only as The Girl with Black Hair through the streets of Kyoto’s famed Ponto-Cho party district, drinking middle-aged salarymen under the table when she’s not mixing with barflies, obsessive collectors, and guerilla theater performers, all the while oblivious to the efforts of a fellow student who has been creating increasingly fantastic and contrived reasons to run into her in a gambit to win her love. A comic fable of fleeting youthful passions, as lived out through one mad, unforgettable night.

screenings.title: The Green Room
screenings.description: One of Truffaut’s most personal and beautiful films, photographed “in fecund greens and withering yellows” [Dave Kehr, Chicago Reader] by DP Néstor Almendros, and one of the least known of Truffaut’s major works—audiences, it seems, weren’t ready for this stark rumination on death from a filmmaker known for his gentle humor and twinkling personability. Truffaut, not far removed from his own premature end, stars himself alongside Nathalie Baye in this adaptation of Henry James’s short story “Altar of the Dead,” about a newspaper obituary writer who has become obsessed with the memory of friends departed from this mortal coil, represented here by images of the director’s own deceased loved ones.

screenings.title: Wake in Fright
screenings.description: It’s the eve of the Christmas holiday, and polite, young middle-class schoolteacher John Grant (Gary Bond), tied to a position at a tiny township in the outback, is on his way to Sydney to see his girlfriend by way of a stopoff in the grubby mining burg Bundanyabba (“The Yabba” to locals) when he pops into the pub for a drink… Five days of debauchery with local degenerates Donald Pleasence and Chips Rafferty later, the fresh-faced Grant has been replaced by a desperate, unshaven, beer-and-booze-pickled maniac, acquainted with species of depravity he could scarcely have imagined a week ago, and with the barbaric rites of the bush. A furious fever dream from Canuck director Kotcheff, who knew a thing or two about chronic self-degradation as practiced in far-flung outposts of the British Commonwealth, and one of the greatest of Australian films.

screenings.title: Drunken Master II
screenings.description: Sixteen years after starring in Yuen Woo-ping’s Drunken Master, the film that cemented its star’s place as the clown prince of martial arts cinema, Jackie Chan returned to the role of bibulous warrior Wong Fei-hung (aka “Freddie Wong”) with Lau in the director’s chair, the result nothing less than a masterclass in breathless kung-fu action. Fei-hung faces off against a shadowy syndicate siphoning precious artifacts out of the Chinese Mainland—and jabberjaw stepmother Anita Mui—in this bonanza of stunning set piece after stunning set piece, climaxing in a 20-minute grand finale that is one of the pinnacles of go-for-broke Hong Kong moviemaking. (After watching it, a cowed Roger Ebert opined, “It may not be possible to film a better fight scene.” We concur.)

screenings.description: “In L’Argent I sense an unconditional surrender to despair and disgust. One can hardly argue that contemporary humanity does not deserve its full quotient of despair and disgust. And it is not even a matter of this social system or that. The rottenness seems to have plunged very deeply into the universal psyche. The artist, however is still obligated to search for order amid the chaos, for beauty amid the ugliness, for truth amid the falsehoods, and, above all, for hope amid the despair… That a filmmaker can lift us to these levels of contemplation and speculation is proof enough of that filmmaker’s greatness” —Andrew Sarris

screenings.title: JFK
screenings.description: The alpha and omega of conspiracy films, Stone’s deliriously entertaining cinematic inquest stars Kevin Costner as Jim Garrison, the New Orleans district attorney who came to find the circumstances of the 35th US president’s assassination more than a little fishy and got to digging around. Gary Oldman, as “patsy” Lee Harvey Oswald, stands out in a supporting cast teeming with familiar faces, including Tommy Lee Jones swishing it up as Louisiana businessman Clay Shaw, Brian Doyle-Murray as Jack Ruby, Donald Sutherland as whistleblower “Mr. X,” and Garrison himself as Justice Earl Warren. “A knockout. Part history book, part comic book, the movie rushes toward judgment for three breathless hours, lassoing facts and factoids by the thousands, then bundling them together into an incendiary device that would frag any viewer's complacency… Tip-top tabloid journalism. In its bravura and breadth, JFK is seditiously enthralling; in its craft, wondrously complex.” —Richard Corliss, Time

screenings.title: Rambling Rose
screenings.description: Acclaimed novelist and screenwriter Calder Willingham adapted his own 1972 novel of the same name scripting Coolidge’s tender, deeply humane Great Depression-set drama, starring Dern as Rose, a teenager rescued from a life of prostitution after being taken in as a domestic by an eccentric Georgia family, her sexual precocity soon making her a destabilizing force in the household, comprised of father Robert Duvall, mother Diane Ladd, and son Lukas Haas. Dern and Ladd would become the first real-life mother-daughter duo to be nominated for acting Academy Awards in the same year for their work in Rambling Rose, which Roger Ebert raved “contains some of the best performances of the year, especially in the ensemble acting of the four main characters.”

screenings.title: Mountains of the Moon
screenings.description: William Harrison’s 1982 historical novel about 19th-century explorers Richard Francis Burton and John Hanning Speke and their rival expeditions to discover the source of the Nile River received a suitably epic treatment from Rafelson (Five Easy Pieces, The Postman Always Rings Twice), whose beautifully detailed dual-portrait character study follows the two men, played by Patrick Bergin and Iain Glen, from London drawing rooms and lecture halls to the perilous wilds of Central Africa. “Completely absorbing. It tells its story soberly and intelligently, and with quiet style. It doesn’t manufacture false thrills or phony excitement… [A film] about the unquenchable compulsion of some men to see what is beyond the horizon, and about the hunger for glory.” —Roger Ebert, Chicago Sun-Times

screenings.title: Rebecca
screenings.description: “Last night I dreamt I went to Manderlay again…” Hitchcock was still a newly arrived UK import when this gothic thriller/romance, based on the novel of the same title by Daphne du Maurier, took Outstanding Production (later “Best Picture”) honors at the Academy Awards. Joan Fontaine stars as a terribly self-conscious young woman, never identified by name, who becomes enamored with a saturnine, aristocratic widower, Maxim de Winter (Laurence Olivier, fresh from Wuthering Heights)—and, once she’s been taken as his bride, obsessed with his late wife’s phantom presence in their home on the Cornwall coast. A marvel of directorial assurance that turns the screws with poise and panache.

screenings.title: Stavisky
screenings.description: From money laundering to influence peddling, casino gambling to dabbling in controversial politics, the life of Serge Alexandre, aka Stavisky, flashes before our eyes and we see the making and unmaking of the theatrically charming con artist who used turn-of-the-century France as his playground. Resnais’s biographical drama features the late Jean-Paul Belmondo, in one of his greatest roles, as the eponymous swindler, a real-life adventurer whose 1934 death remains a mystery to this day; Anny Duperey, as his wife; a standout Charles Boyer, in his penultimate performance, as his nobleman friend; and music by Stephen Sondheim, contributing his only full-length film score.

screenings.title: Millionaires' Express
screenings.description: Arguably the most formidable ensemble cast in the history of Hong Kong cinema assembled on the set of Hung’s Eastern Western, in which reformed outlaw Sammo teams with Sheriff (played by Yuen Biao) to protect their impoverished rural hometown from a sudden influx of desperate characters, all plotting to make a fast fortune off the passengers of a brand new luxury train scheduled to pass through on the Shanghai-Chengdu line. Veteran stalwarts like Jimmy Wang Yu and James Tien rub shoulders with fresh talents like Rosamund Kwan and Cynthia Rothrock, Japanese ninjas vie with Soviet bandits, and the spectacular action and inspired slapstick scarcely lets up for a minute in this deliriously entertaining action-adventure vaudeville.

screenings.title: Made in Hong Kong
screenings.description: The first independent film released in post-Handover Hong Kong, Chan’s atmospheric shoestring-budget character study is a rough-and-ready piece of work shot on grainy leftover 35mm short ends in the city’s overcrowded subsidized housing projects. The result is a tough, pessimistic film, a portrait of a city on the brink that follows the drifting of high-school dropout and wannabe Triad tough Autumn Moon (Sam Lee, in a star-making role, opposite a largely nonprofessional cast), who sees little hope for his future or that of his home as a newly created Special Administrative Region within China. A raw, groundbreaking drama and portrait of nihilistic youth in the same vein as Rebel Without a Cause, My Own Private Idaho, and The Doom Generation, the film poses questions that remain burningly relevant as tumult engulfs Hong Kong.

screenings.title: First Blood
screenings.description: The movie whose runaway success singlehandedly landed Carolco in the ranks of legit Tinseltown players, Kotcheff’s taut adaptation of David Morrell’s 1972 novel of the same name introduces Sylvester Stallone as burnt-out Vietnam vet John Rambo, in the words of critic J. Hoberman, a combination of “super-grunt, Green Beret, hippie protester, VC guerilla, righteous outlaw [and] Hollywood Freedom Fighter.” Arriving in the town of Hope, Washington State, after paying his respects to an old army buddy who’s died from the lingering effects of Agent Orange exposure, Rambo is escorted to the city limits by hard-ass local sheriff Brian Dennehy who, with this slight, unwittingly lights the fuse on a human stick of dynamite. As Colonel Trautman (Richard Crenna), Rambo’s old superior officer, says upon arriving in Hope to prevent a slaughter: “I didn’t come to save Rambo from you. I came to save you from Rambo.”

screenings.title: Dumplings
screenings.description: Expanding his segment of the same name in the horror anthology film Three… Extremes, Chan’s Dumplings tells the deliciously deviant tale of ex-soap star Mrs. Li (Miriam Yeung) who, her looks fading and husband Tony Leung Ka-fai’s eye wandering, begins supplementing her diet with a special preparation of the eponymous foodstuff that uses the flesh of unborn fetuses for filling. Christopher Doyle’s photography, along with the work of production designer Yee Chung-man, provide an elegant setting to this baleful, bleak fable described by its director as a “post-feminist horror movie,” a work that may or may not have exercised its influence on a little picture called The Substance.

screenings.title: Possession
screenings.description: Easily the most harrowing divorce drama ever made, Zuławski’s one-of-a-kind genre pastiche has spy Sam Neill returning to his Berlin home from a mission abroad to discover that wife Isabelle Adjani wants suddenly to split up. Launching an investigation into the reasons for her ever-more-alarming behavior, he discovers a truth more sinister (and nauseating) than his wildest suspicions, as Zuławski’s highly-choreographed cinematic delirium and Andrzej Korzyński’s pulsating score push things light years past over-the-top. Adjani won a César for her performance, one of the most grueling ever caught on film, though later reflected that the palpable ordeal she put herself through on the movie was nearly enough to make her leave acting behind.

screenings.title: Good Morning
screenings.description: Two brothers in a modern Japanese suburb go on strike to bring their parents to their knees and achieve their cherished dream: owning a television set for watching sumo matches. While borrowing from his own classic I Was Born, But… (1932), Ozu turns in a decidedly contemporary, family-friendly satire of a pop-culture colonized country seen in lively Agfacolor, which also functions as the single best showcase for the master’s fondness for fart jokes.

screenings.title: The Triplets of Belleville
screenings.description: This animated film follows elderly Frenchwoman Madame Souza as she becomes involved in international intrigue when her grandson, Champion, a professional cyclist, is kidnapped and taken abroad. Joined by her faithful dog, Bruno, Souza embarks on a journey to find Champion, and stumbles across unlikely allies in the form of three sisters who are veterans of the vaudeville stage. Tracking down Champion's criminal captors, the quartet of old women use their wits to try and win the day.

screenings.title: Stavisky
screenings.description: From money laundering to influence peddling, casino gambling to dabbling in controversial politics, the life of Serge Alexandre, aka Stavisky, flashes before our eyes and we see the making and unmaking of the theatrically charming con artist who used turn-of-the-century France as his playground. Resnais’s biographical drama features the late Jean-Paul Belmondo, in one of his greatest roles, as the eponymous swindler, a real-life adventurer whose 1934 death remains a mystery to this day; Anny Duperey, as his wife; a standout Charles Boyer, in his penultimate performance, as his nobleman friend; and music by Stephen Sondheim, contributing his only full-length film score.

screenings.title: Sholay
screenings.description: Sippy’s sprawling “curry Western,” blown up to 70mm for first-run distribution and shot over the course of two-and-a-half years in the rugged hills around the city of Ramanagara, was one of the most ambitious undertakings in Bollywood history: star-studded (including a young Amjad Khan giving a villainous dacoit for the ages), with earworm tunes courtesy legendary writing team Salim-Javed and composer R.D. Burman. India’s all-time box-office champion for nearly 20 years, having logged a storied unbroken five-year run at Mumbai’s Minerva cinema, this ripping yarn about a former lawman (Sanjeev Kumar) recruiting two petty crooks (Amitabh Bachchan and Dharmendra) to help him bring down a beastly bandit who’s terrorizing the village of Ramgarh can now be seen with its astonishing original ending, censored on initial release, restored.

screenings.title: FC Live: Jonah Who Will Be 25 in the Year 2000
screenings.description: "Perhaps best known as the host of Ways of Seeing, the 1972 BBC program that introduced a generation to the ideological analysis of visual art, John Berger was one of the most important writers of the last century. Across an oeuvre comprising modernist novels, breathtaking analyses of painting and photography, reports on life in Palestine, correspondences with revolutionaries like Subcomandante Marcos, and much else, Berger’s generosity, intelligence, and uncompromising integrity made him an exemplary left-wing public intellectual. A committed Marxist all his life, he was the rare critic for whom art was, always and necessarily, a site of both power and beauty; he was proud of being called a political propagandist, he said, 'but my heart and eye have remained that of a painter.'" —Film Comment

screenings.title: L'Argent
screenings.description: “In L’Argent I sense an unconditional surrender to despair and disgust. One can hardly argue that contemporary humanity does not deserve its full quotient of despair and disgust. And it is not even a matter of this social system or that. The rottenness seems to have plunged very deeply into the universal psyche. The artist, however is still obligated to search for order amid the chaos, for beauty amid the ugliness, for truth amid the falsehoods, and, above all, for hope amid the despair… That a filmmaker can lift us to these levels of contemplation and speculation is proof enough of that filmmaker’s greatness” —Andrew Sarris

screenings.title: The Eight Diagram Pole Fighter
screenings.description: Made as the declining Shaw Brothers Studio entered its twilight years, Lau’s Eight Diagram Pole Fighter, inspired by Song dynasty folklore, has all the radiant beauty of a spectacular sunset, a showcase for all that the Shaw machine, at the height of its fine-tuned powers, did best. Six of his seven brothers and his general father slaughtered in an ambush by Khitan barbarians, Yang Wu-lang (Gordon Liu) finds asylum at a Buddhist monastery in Mount Wutai, where he practices and develops the eponymous technique, and learns to abjure violence—though his vows of pacifism will be sorely tested when his family’s butchers resurface. “One of the most impressive of [Lau’s] last Shaw works… A somber dissection of the revenge motif… Lau’s sympathy seems largely with the monks who insist, in film after film, that revenge debases the martial arts.” —David Bordwell, Planet Hong Kong

screenings.title: The Green Room
screenings.description: One of Truffaut’s most personal and beautiful films, photographed “in fecund greens and withering yellows” [Dave Kehr, Chicago Reader] by DP Néstor Almendros, and one of the least known of Truffaut’s major works—audiences, it seems, weren’t ready for this stark rumination on death from a filmmaker known for his gentle humor and twinkling personability. Truffaut, not far removed from his own premature end, stars himself alongside Nathalie Baye in this adaptation of Henry James’s short story “Altar of the Dead,” about a newspaper obituary writer who has become obsessed with the memory of friends departed from this mortal coil, represented here by images of the director’s own deceased loved ones.

screenings.title: Wake in Fright
screenings.description: It’s the eve of the Christmas holiday, and polite, young middle-class schoolteacher John Grant (Gary Bond), tied to a position at a tiny township in the outback, is on his way to Sydney to see his girlfriend by way of a stopoff in the grubby mining burg Bundanyabba (“The Yabba” to locals) when he pops into the pub for a drink… Five days of debauchery with local degenerates Donald Pleasence and Chips Rafferty later, the fresh-faced Grant has been replaced by a desperate, unshaven, beer-and-booze-pickled maniac, acquainted with species of depravity he could scarcely have imagined a week ago, and with the barbaric rites of the bush. A furious fever dream from Canuck director Kotcheff, who knew a thing or two about chronic self-degradation as practiced in far-flung outposts of the British Commonwealth, and one of the greatest of Australian films.

screenings.title: Drunken Master II
screenings.description: Sixteen years after starring in Yuen Woo-ping’s Drunken Master, the film that cemented its star’s place as the clown prince of martial arts cinema, Jackie Chan returned to the role of bibulous warrior Wong Fei-hung (aka “Freddie Wong”) with Lau in the director’s chair, the result nothing less than a masterclass in breathless kung-fu action. Fei-hung faces off against a shadowy syndicate siphoning precious artifacts out of the Chinese Mainland—and jabberjaw stepmother Anita Mui—in this bonanza of stunning set piece after stunning set piece, climaxing in a 20-minute grand finale that is one of the pinnacles of go-for-broke Hong Kong moviemaking. (After watching it, a cowed Roger Ebert opined, “It may not be possible to film a better fight scene.” We concur.)

screenings.title: Vertigo
screenings.description: Dress up becomes a matter of fevered fixation in Hitchcock’s utterly intoxicating thriller, in which ex-cop-cum-snoop-for-hire Scottie Ferguson (Jimmy Stewart) sets out on a routine job tailing the mysterious Madeline (Kim Novak), an old pal’s wife—and soon finds himself in the center of a whirlpool of romantic obsession and supernatural quandaries, speeding towards a tragic denouement. Perennially on the short list of the greatest films of all time, Hitchcock’s film of death, desire, and doppelgangers—a key inspiration haunting every frame of Chantal Akerman's La Captive—has lost none of its ability to simultaneously seduce and repel. “One of the landmarks—not merely of the movies, but of 20th-century art.”—Dave Kehr, Chicago Reader

screenings.title: Chocolat
screenings.description: After years of honing her craft as assistant director for the likes of Jim Jarmusch and Wim Wenders, Denis emerged as a filmmaker with a distinct and fully-formed sense of her art in this, her sensual and infinitely sensitive semi-autobiographical feature debut, drawing on memories of a childhood spent in French-occupied Africa. In Cameroon, civil servant François Cluzet comes and goes on his appointed rounds, while his young daughter and neglected wife (Giulia Boschi) gravitate ever closer to their house servant, Protée (Isaach de Bankolé) in his absence, and the murmurs of anti-colonial resistance increase in vehemence away from eavesdropping whites. “Some kind of miniature classic.”—Vincent Canby, The New York Times

screenings.title: Conversation Piece
screenings.description: Burt Lancaster reunited with his The Leopard director for Visconti’s penultimate film, an elegant odd-couple chamber drama in which the leonine “Boit” plays a graying American intellectual immured from the modern world in his Roman palazzo—until, that is, his fortress of solitude is invaded by a pushy Marquise (Silvana Mangano) who browbears him into renting her his unused top floor to be used as a gilded cage for her boytoy, Konrad (Helmut Berger), a ’68 activist turned gigolo to the gentry, who interrupts the old man’s bedtime Mozart with Italopop and nude pot parties. Best known for his work in the epic vein, Visconti here renders verbal close-combat every bit as thrilling as any dispatch from the battlefields of Europe.

screenings.title: Paranoid Park
screenings.description: Adapting Blake Nelson’s Y.A. novel of the same name, Van Sant renders the youth gathering place of the skate park a voluptuous dreamscape with the help of cinematographers Chris Doyle and Rain Kathy Li. Teenaged skate rat Alex—Gabe Nevins, leading a largely amateur cast recruited via MySpace—finds himself a prime suspect in the death of a security guard, silently carrying a crushing burden of knowledge through his daily rounds, a contrast to the gravity-defying liberation he finds carving it up at “Paranoid Park.”

screenings.title: The Milk of Sorrow
screenings.description: Winner of the Golden Bear at the 59th Berlin International Film Festival, Llosa’s formidable sophomore feature focuses on Fausta (Magaly Solier, in a performance nearly free of dialogue), the only daughter of an aged Indigenous Peruvian woman who, following her mother’s death, must negotiate arrangements for her burial as well as negotiate the smothering legacy of trauma that her parent, horribly misused during the Shining Path terrorist insurgencies of the 1980s and ’90s, has left behind with her child even after herself departing this mortal coil. “Littered with unforgettable images of incongruity, destruction, and, finally, healing” [The Village Voice], The Milk of Sorrow is an exquisitely shot study in inherited injury guarded like a precious heirloom, a work of tragic magic realism.

screenings.title: Hannibal
screenings.description: Hopkins reprises his role from 1991’s The Silence of the Lambs as psychiatrist-turned-cannibal serial killer Hannibal Lecter in Scott’s follow-up, a gristly fairy tale that finds FBI special agent Clarice Starling (Julianne Moore, ably taking on the role originated by Jodie Foster) racing against time to find to catch up with her old foil before he’s located by Mason R. Verger (Gary Oldman), a sadistic scion of enormous wealth who, after years earlier being grotesquely mutilated by Lecter, has dedicated the entirety of his power and influence towards a terrible and extravagant dream of vengeance. Unidentified in promotional materials and unbilled until the film’s closing credits, wholly unrecognizable under a prosthetic mask, and stripped of almost every expressive tool an actor traditionally relies upon to practice their craft, Oldman offers up an indelible portrayal of utter and absolute human corruption.

screenings.title: Scene of the Crime
screenings.description: One of seven collaborations between Téchiné and Catherine Deneuve, Scene of the Crime is a study of domestic discontent wearing the trappings of a boilerplate thriller, its action set into motion when a disconsolate 13-year-old boy runs across a fugitive criminal (Wadeck Stanczak) while loitering in a village cemetery, an encounter that will have immense repercussions for his woebegone mother, Lili (Deneuve), her manipulative estranged husband (Victor Lanoux), and Lili’s own overbearing mother (Danielle Darrieux, César nominated for her work here.) “The crux of the film is the mother-son relationship, and it is drawn in painful accuracy… An imaginatively structured, highly cinematic experience in which we watch with detachment the workings of fate unravel with a swift yet oddly calm inevitability.” —Los Angeles Times

screenings.title: Good Morning
screenings.description: Two brothers in a modern Japanese suburb go on strike to bring their parents to their knees and achieve their cherished dream: owning a television set for watching sumo matches. While borrowing from his own classic I Was Born, But… (1932), Ozu turns in a decidedly contemporary, family-friendly satire of a pop-culture colonized country seen in lively Agfacolor, which also functions as the single best showcase for the master’s fondness for fart jokes.

screenings.title: Le amiche
screenings.description: Perhaps the first of Antonioni’s films to give a clear indication of the direction of his mature style, this adaptation of Cesare Pavese’s Among Women Only finds glamorous Eleonora Rossi Drago returning to her hometown of Turin to open a branch of a fashion boutique, in the process taking up with the miserable, sniping local smart set and beginning an affair with architect’s assistant Franco Fabrizi. The air of bourgeois discontentment is thick, while the disquieting train station finale is the first of Antonioni’s great set pieces.

screenings.title: The Warriors
screenings.description: “Waaarriors! Come out and play-ay!” Falsely accused of responsibility for the assassination of New York’s most powerful ganglord during a citywide summit in the Bronx’s Van Cortlandt Park, Swan (Michael Beck) and his fellow Warriors now have to fight their way back, block by block and mano a mano, to the safe shores of their Coney Island turf. The film’s knuckle-busting action choreography and its vision of NYC as a coliseum-like proving grounds for epic heroism—its source, at a distance, is Xenophon’s 4th century BC Anabasis—are delectable, but its greatness lies in its attention to character, how it lets us see a crew of provincial Brooklynites gradually discovering they’re the toughest dudes in town.

screenings.description: After years of honing her craft as assistant director for the likes of Jim Jarmusch and Wim Wenders, Denis emerged as a filmmaker with a distinct and fully-formed sense of her art in this, her sensual and infinitely sensitive semi-autobiographical feature debut, drawing on memories of a childhood spent in French-occupied Africa. screenings.title: The Chaser
screenings.description: Drawing inspiration from the gristly exploits of South Korean serial killer Yoo Young-chul, Na’s astonishingly assured directorial debut stars Ha Jung-woo as a sadistic killer, Ji Yeong-min, and Kim Yoon-seok as Joong-ho, an ex-detective with a checkered past now running a prostitution ring. After helplessly watching his stable of employees disappear and dwindle, Joong-ho sets out to find the sicko responsible—and in the course of a sleepless night of cat and mouse, finds he has to contend not only with the killer’s calculating intelligence and red herring misleads, but with an incompetent police force and a thicket of bureaucratic barriers that seem to have been erected with the specific purpose of allowing the guilty to get away clean. Winner of Best Actor, Best Film, and Best Director at Korea’s Grand Bell Awards, The Chaser is both a precision-tuned white-knuckle thriller and an agonized exploration of insoluble moral conundrums.

screenings.title: Otar Iosseliani Early Shorts Program
screenings.description: A program of the inspired early shorts that established Iosseliani at the forefront of a new, rising generation of Georgian filmmakers. Featuring Akvarel, in which a quarreling working-class couple experience a revelation at an art exhibition; Sapovnela, in which an old man who tends exquisite flower gardens in the hills around Mtskheta sees his life’s work threatened by the arrival of a new road; April, in which a young couple find their happiness dwindling as their comfort increases upon moving into a brand new, squeaky clean housing development, and Tudzhi (Cast Iron), a documentary description of life in an ironworks that singles out individuals on the factory floor not as symbols of thrumming Soviet industrial might, but as human beings.

screenings.title: Favorites of the Moon
screenings.description: Having relocated to France in 1982, Iosseliani wasted no time in showing the world he hadn’t left his singular gifts behind upon leaving Georgia, taking home the Special Jury Prize at the 41st Venice International Film Festival for this puckish panoramic comedy about dizzying reversals of fortune and everyday acts of larceny, petty and otherwise. Terrorists, chanteuses, antique dealers, police inspectors, street walkers, and street sweepers all have a part to play in this farcical fable located at the intersection of Dickens and Tati, which follows the circulation of two precious objects—a Limoges porcelain dinner service and a portrait of a Belle Époque–era aristocratic beauty—as they’re passed from one pair of hands to another, and up and down the socioeconomic hierarchy, in Paris’s 13th arrondissement. Co-written with regular Polanski collaborator Gérard Brach, and featuring a very fresh-faced Mathieu Amalric in his very first film role.

screenings.title: Girlhood
screenings.description: Set in the suburbs of Paris, Sciamma’s coming-of-age story stars Karidja Touré as Marieme, a 16-year-old who finds a sense of sorority, camaraderie, and mutual support when she joins up with an amateur “gang” of girls her age—much to the chagrin of her overbearing, abusive brother. A harsh but cautiously hopeful depiction of the lives of young Afro-French women, and the unique adversities they face.

screenings.title: Millennium Mambo
screenings.description: A stylish and seductive submersion into the techno-scored neon nightlife of Taipei, Hou’s much-misunderstood marvel stars Shu Qi (The Assassin) as an aimless bar hostess drifting away from her blowhard boyfriend and towards Jack Kao’s suave, sensitive gangster. Structured as a flashback to the then-present from the then-future of 2011, it’s a transfixing trance-out of a movie, drenched in club lights, ecstatic endorphin-rush exhilaration, and a nagging undercurrent of ennui. Hou and longtime cinematographer Lee here break from their familiar pattern of elegantly composed long shot long takes to create something both more intimate and hectic, a film whose shallow-focus images, jittery camerawork, and cramped locations evoke both the claustrophobic character of Taiwan’s capital city and, in Lee’s words, “the feeling of youth.”

screenings.title: In the Mood for Love
screenings.description: Wong’s arthouse smash is the very simple tale of two people in early ’60s Hong Kong, Mr. Chow (Tony Leung Chiu-wai) and Mrs. Chen (Maggie Cheung), drawn to one another by the discovery that their spouses are getting together on the side. A little story, full of little details, all surrounding a love affair that isn’t really a love affair—but throbbing with huge, aching emotions that it can barely contain. It might just break your heart.

screenings.title: A Day in the Country + People on Sunday
screenings.director: Robert Siodmak, Jean Renoir , Edgar G. Ulmer
screenings.description: Two slices of life from Europe entre deux guerres, and two compact masterpieces. Renoir’s featurette fragment, based on a Guy de Maupassant short story and only edited 10 years after its shoot came to a premature end, evokes the disappeared world of Belle Époque France—the world of Renoir’s father, the painter Pierre-Auguste—by describing an afternoon’s outing for two young shirt-chasers, a middle-aged Paris shopkeeper, and the shopkeeper’s susceptible-to-flattery wife and daughter. People on Sunday, made by a supergroup brain trust of future cinematic luminaries including Billy Wilder, Fred Zinnemann, Robert Siodmak, and Edgar G. Ulmer, follows a quintet of Berliners through a weekend of walks along the Wannsee, domestic squabbles, and frisky flirtation. Modest in ambition, yet they contain the world in miniature.

screenings.title: Mountains of the Moon
screenings.description: William Harrison’s 1982 historical novel about 19th-century explorers Richard Francis Burton and John Hanning Speke and their rival expeditions to discover the source of the Nile River received a suitably epic treatment from Rafelson (Five Easy Pieces, The Postman Always Rings Twice), whose beautifully detailed dual-portrait character study follows the two men, played by Patrick Bergin and Iain Glen, from London drawing rooms and lecture halls to the perilous wilds of Central Africa. “Completely absorbing. It tells its story soberly and intelligently, and with quiet style. It doesn’t manufacture false thrills or phony excitement… [A film] about the unquenchable compulsion of some men to see what is beyond the horizon, and about the hunger for glory.” —Roger Ebert, Chicago Sun-Times

screenings.title: Rebecca
screenings.description: “Last night I dreamt I went to Manderlay again…” Hitchcock was still a newly arrived UK import when this gothic thriller/romance, based on the novel of the same title by Daphne du Maurier, took Outstanding Production (later “Best Picture”) honors at the Academy Awards. Joan Fontaine stars as a terribly self-conscious young woman, never identified by name, who becomes enamored with a saturnine, aristocratic widower, Maxim de Winter (Laurence Olivier, fresh from Wuthering Heights)—and, once she’s been taken as his bride, obsessed with his late wife’s phantom presence in their home on the Cornwall coast. A marvel of directorial assurance that turns the screws with poise and panache.

screenings.title: Conversation Piece
screenings.description: Burt Lancaster reunited with his The Leopard director for Visconti’s penultimate film, an elegant odd-couple chamber drama in which the leonine “Boit” plays a graying American intellectual immured from the modern world in his Roman palazzo—until, that is, his fortress of solitude is invaded by a pushy Marquise (Silvana Mangano) who browbears him into renting her his unused top floor to be used as a gilded cage for her boytoy, Konrad (Helmut Berger), a ’68 activist turned gigolo to the gentry, who interrupts the old man’s bedtime Mozart with Italopop and nude pot parties. Best known for his work in the epic vein, Visconti here renders verbal close-combat every bit as thrilling as any dispatch from the battlefields of Europe.

screenings.title: And Then There Was Light
screenings.description: The confrontation of a traditional rural/agrarian culture bound to the land and the cycles of the seasons and an urban/industrial society that has largely forgotten these ties, an abiding concern of Iosseliani’s cinema, plays out against a backdrop entirely new to his work in this fable-like homage to silent cinema, intertitles and all. In the village of Casamance in southern Senegal, home to the Jola people, life goes on much as it has since time immemorial, with its gossip-mongering, its local scandals, its rituals of field labor and midday meals—until, that is, new European machinery begins to arrive on the scene, its intended use: deforestation of the region and exploitation of its natural resources. “There is an interweaving, an interdependence, of real life and ancient poetry… The film’s texture is not raw, not naturalistic. In Africa, as in his native Georgia, [Iosseliani] enters into a kind of symbiosis with the ‘spirit’ of the country.” —Le Monde

screenings.title: The Chaser
screenings.description: Drawing inspiration from the gristly exploits of South Korean serial killer Yoo Young-chul, Na’s astonishingly assured directorial debut stars Ha Jung-woo as a sadistic killer, Ji Yeong-min, and Kim Yoon-seok as Joong-ho, an ex-detective with a checkered past now running a prostitution ring. After helplessly watching his stable of employees disappear and dwindle, Joong-ho sets out to find the sicko responsible—and in the course of a sleepless night of cat and mouse, finds he has to contend not only with the killer’s calculating intelligence and red herring misleads, but with an incompetent police force and a thicket of bureaucratic barriers that seem to have been erected with the specific purpose of allowing the guilty to get away clean. Winner of Best Actor, Best Film, and Best Director at Korea’s Grand Bell Awards, The Chaser is both a precision-tuned white-knuckle thriller and an agonized exploration of insoluble moral conundrums.

screenings.title: Scene of the Crime
screenings.description: One of seven collaborations between Téchiné and Catherine Deneuve, Scene of the Crime is a study of domestic discontent wearing the trappings of a boilerplate thriller, its action set into motion when a disconsolate 13-year-old boy runs across a fugitive criminal (Wadeck Stanczak) while loitering in a village cemetery, an encounter that will have immense repercussions for his woebegone mother, Lili (Deneuve), her manipulative estranged husband (Victor Lanoux), and Lili’s own overbearing mother (Danielle Darrieux, César nominated for her work here.) “The crux of the film is the mother-son relationship, and it is drawn in painful accuracy… An imaginatively structured, highly cinematic experience in which we watch with detachment the workings of fate unravel with a swift yet oddly calm inevitability.” —Los Angeles Times

screenings.title: Les Bonnes Femmes
screenings.description: An early and enormous artistic triumph of the French New Wave, Chabrol’s quietly class-conscious film records the dreams, dramas, and self-deceptions of a quartet of young Parisian girls working at an appliance shop, among them Bernadette Lafont and Stéphane Audran. A study of the social habits of the petite bourgeoisie, set against indubitably authentic locations seen in crisp black-and-white courtesy DP Henri Decaë, which develops into a melancholy cautionary tale on the risks of romantic illusion.

screenings.title: The Warriors
screenings.description: “Waaarriors! Come out and play-ay!” Falsely accused of responsibility for the assassination of New York’s most powerful ganglord during a citywide summit in the Bronx’s Van Cortlandt Park, Swan (Michael Beck) and his fellow Warriors now have to fight their way back, block by block and mano a mano, to the safe shores of their Coney Island turf. The film’s knuckle-busting action choreography and its vision of NYC as a coliseum-like proving grounds for epic heroism—its source, at a distance, is Xenophon’s 4th century BC Anabasis—are delectable, but its greatness lies in its attention to character, how it lets us see a crew of provincial Brooklynites gradually discovering they’re the toughest dudes in town.

screenings.title: La Notte
screenings.description: Novelist Giovanni Pontano (Marcello Mastroianni) is the toast of the Italian literary scene, but smothered by the trappings of success. His misery weighs heavily on his wife, Lidia (Jeanne Moreau), already carrying her own cargo of existential anguish. In the course of a day and a night—spent at a hospital sickroom, a book launch, a nightclub, and a party at an industrialist’s villa, where Giovanni flirts extensively with the host’s daughter, Valentina (Monica Vitti)—the couple must come to terms with the extinction of the love that once existed between them… or not? A film steeped in despair but thrilling in its adventurous, architectonic use of the cinematic medium, from its opening credits—an avant-jazz/musique concrète overture accompanying the industrialized Milanese cityscape—to its beguiling final scene.

screenings.title: Deliverance
screenings.description: A quartet of city slicker businessman buddies (Jon Voight, Ned Beatty, Ronny Cox and, in a star-making role, Burt Reynolds) leave Atlanta to head into the Georgia backwoods for what’s meant to be a little weekend canoe trip… and stumble headlong instead into the hidden horrors lurking in the old Southland. The trial-by-fire endurance test that they’ll pass through makes for pure, pulse-pounding cinema, with at least three scenes—the “Dueling Banjos” gas station stop, Beatty’s “Squeal like a pig!” humiliation, and the white-water rapids set piece—that rank above the most remembered in ’70s American cinema.

screenings.title: Nil by Mouth
screenings.description: Set in the hardscrabble South London of the filmmaker’s own youth and dedicated—in a more than slightly ambivalent gesture—to the memory of his father, Gary Oldman’s disarmingly raw debut as writer/director/producer flings us into a working-class family’s lives of profane squabbling and substance abuse as lived in the pressure cooker of a council estate flat: tyrannical father Ray (Ray Winstone); long-suffering wife, Val (Kathy Burke); Val’s junkie brother, Billy (Charlie Creed-Miles); Val’s mother and grandmother (Oldman’s sister, billed as Laila Morse, and Edna Doré); and the couple’s young daughter, who has no choice but to soak in the ambient trauma of her surroundings. “Unflinching and observant… There is humor in it, and tender insight… We sense Oldman’s ability to understand, if not forgive.” —Roger Ebert, Chicago Sun-Times

screenings.title: Walkabout
screenings.description: Having fled into the Outback after their father has a psychotic episode that threatens their very lives, two Sydney-bred adolescent siblings (Jenny Agutter and Luc Roeg, the director’s son) meet an Aboriginal teenager (David Gulpilil, in his debut role) on his traditional “walkabout”—a rite-of-passage journey, undertaken in solitude—who aids them in adjusting to the apparently harsh, unforgiving landscape around them, a landscape that, as Walkabout progresses, is heavily romanticised, revealing an Edenic splendor lurking beneath its sun-baked surface. A foundational text of the Australian New Wave and a film of genuinely awe-striking natural beauty, shot by cinematographer-turned-director Roeg himself.

screenings.title: The Hunger
screenings.description: A lush vampire romance with sex and style to spare, much of it provided by stars Catherine Deneuve and David Bowie as a couple of posh, centuries-old nightclubbing New York bloodsuckers who, when one begins to show the first signs of aging, recruit assistance from Susan Sarandon’s geriatrics researcher, then find themselves in a very, very attractive throuple. Yes, that’s “Bela Lugosi’s Dead” artists Bauhaus in a brief cameo.

screenings.title: Obsession
screenings.description: De Palma’s twisted twist on Hitchcock’s Vertigo stars Cliff Robertson as a wealthy New Orleans real-estate developer still mourning the loss of his beloved wife (Dead Ringers’ Genevieve Bujold) and daughter years after their abductions until, on a visit to Florence, he encounters her exact double. (In addition to Hitch, screenwriter Paul Schrader drew inspiration from Dante and his infatuation with muse Beatrice.) With lusciously gauzy cinematography by Vilmos Zsigmond, a richly romantic score by Hitch regular Bernard Herrmann, and Big Easy Baroque location shooting, this is moviemaking as ultrarich confection, a swooning transport “to a more romantic era… and the simple, touching pleasures denied the audience by the current antiromantic spirit of the movies” [Richard Schickel].

screenings.title: Chungking Express
screenings.description: A hot-shot to the heart, pop masterpiece Chungking Express tells the stories of two lovelorn cops (Takeshi Kaneshiro and Tony Leung) and the women who baffle them (Brigitte Lin and Faye Wong, who contributes a Cantopop cover of The Cranberries’ “Dreams”), its bifurcated structure suggesting the A- and B-sides of a 45. Wong’s international breakthrough introduced new audiences to his rich, sensorial brand of filmmaking, inviting one to disappear into, sink into, live inside, a voluptuary world bigger and brighter than our own—but just as heartbreaking.

screenings.title: Irreversible
screenings.description: Fourteen long sequence shots arranged in reverse chronology take us on a journey from hell to heaven, from nightmarish violence to connubial bliss. In a BDSM club evocatively called Club Rectum, Pierre (Albert Dupontel) dashes in the face of a man who’s just broken the arm of his friend, Marcus (Vincent Cassel), and is preparing to rape him. From this memorable cold open, we see the events leading up to this bloody denouement—an evening that begins (or ends, as it were) as an innocent outing by the two friends and Marcus’s girlfriend, Alex (Monica Bellucci). Not a film to leave the viewer indifferent, to put it very mildly, featuring a positively punitive, bowel-churning soundtrack by Daft Punk’s Thomas Bangalter.

screenings.title: The Dark Knight
screenings.description: The city of Chicago plays an oppressively glum Gotham in Nolan, Christian Bale, and Gary Oldman’s second Batman outing, a film of Langian architectural oppression that pits Bruce Wayne’s alter ego against Heath Ledger’s anarchic Clown Prince of Crime, with Oldman’s Commissioner Gordon the voice of law-and-order in an increasingly Bedlam-like city. Though Oldman may be known for his chameleonic transformations as an actor and his ability to comfortably occupy the skin of vastly different characters, he would in interviews cite Gordon as the character he’d played who is closest to himself: “A good sense of right and wrong… Family man. Just a regular geezer.”

screenings.title: Two by Robb Moss
screenings.description: A pair of films from Moss, a master of first-person documentary and longtime Professor at Harvard’s Department of Art, Film, and Visual Studies, who will join Metrograph for the screening. Riverdogs is Moss’s lyrical, beautifully photographed account of a 35-day trek down the Colorado River, a paean to youth, the natural world, and a fleeting moment in the increasingly distant past. In his confessional The Tourist, Moss meditates—with a wry sense of humor—on the early years of his marriage, his failed attempts to start a family with his new wife, and the daily vicissitudes of professional life as an itinerant freelance cameraman.

screenings.title: Hannibal
screenings.description: Hopkins reprises his role from 1991’s The Silence of the Lambs as psychiatrist-turned-cannibal serial killer Hannibal Lecter in Scott’s follow-up, a gristly fairy tale that finds FBI special agent Clarice Starling (Julianne Moore, ably taking on the role originated by Jodie Foster) racing against time to find to catch up with her old foil before he’s located by Mason R. Verger (Gary Oldman), a sadistic scion of enormous wealth who, after years earlier being grotesquely mutilated by Lecter, has dedicated the entirety of his power and influence towards a terrible and extravagant dream of vengeance. Unidentified in promotional materials and unbilled until the film’s closing credits, wholly unrecognizable under a prosthetic mask, and stripped of almost every expressive tool an actor traditionally relies upon to practice their craft, Oldman offers up an indelible portrayal of utter and absolute human corruption.

screenings.title: The Others
screenings.description: Having enjoyed a palpable international hit with his Abre Los Ojos—picked up for an American remake, under the title Vanilla Sky, by Tom Cruise—Amenábar made his English-language debut with The Others, a dolorous, deftly directed Old Dark House chiller set in the immediate aftermath of World War II, about a devoutly religious Englishwoman (Nicole Kidman, superb) living in a remote home in the Channel Island with her two young, severely photosensitive children and the strange goings-on that begin shortly after she takes on a trio of new servants. “Elegant… Creates more tension from atmosphere alone than most other horror films do from vats full of fake blood.” —The Times of London

screenings.title: Four Adventures of Reinette and Mirabelle
screenings.description: Shot quickly in and around Paris during a production break on Rohmer’s Le Rayon Vert, this breezy, witty film traces the exploits of two young women—one an ethnology student from the city, the other an unsophisticated aspiring artist from the country. Reinette and Mirabelle (played by Joëlle Miquel and Jessica Forde) become instant friends upon meeting in the first of four vignettes that make up the film (“The Blue Hour”), and in their first two days together, they decide to become roommates in Paris. Throughout the three remaining stories, they encounter many of the inevitable characters of a modern city: the impossible waiter (“The Waiter”), the Metro-station hustler (“The Beggar, the Kleptomaniac and the Hustler”), and the snooty gallery owner (“Selling the Painting”). A Metrograph Pictures release

screenings.title: The Jungle Book
screenings.description: Inspired by the adventures of the foundling Mowgli in Rudyard Kipling’s 1894 collection of the same name, The Jungle Book—the final animated Disney feature to be overseen in its production by Uncle Walt—would become one of the studio’s biggest hits, thanks in no small part to its exceptional confluence of vocal talent (yes, that’s George Sanders as the suavely sinister Bengal tiger Shere Khan) and unforgettable songbook, including perennial favorites “The Bare Necessities” and “I Wanna Be Like You (The Monkey Song),” the latter volcanically belted out by none other than jump blues howler extraordinaire Louis Prima. Brisk, breezy, and simply buckets of fun.

screenings.title: Walkabout
screenings.description: Having fled into the Outback after their father has a psychotic episode that threatens their very lives, two Sydney-bred adolescent siblings (Jenny Agutter and Luc Roeg, the director’s son) meet an Aboriginal teenager (David Gulpilil, in his debut role) on his traditional “walkabout”—a rite-of-passage journey, undertaken in solitude—who aids them in adjusting to the apparently harsh, unforgiving landscape around them, a landscape that, as Walkabout progresses, is heavily romanticised, revealing an Edenic splendor lurking beneath its sun-baked surface. screenings.title: Otar Iosseliani Early Shorts Program
screenings.description: A program of the inspired early shorts that established Iosseliani at the forefront of a new, rising generation of Georgian filmmakers. Featuring Akvarel, in which a quarreling working-class couple experience a revelation at an art exhibition; Sapovnela, in which an old man who tends exquisite flower gardens in the hills around Mtskheta sees his life’s work threatened by the arrival of a new road; April, in which a young couple find their happiness dwindling as their comfort increases upon moving into a brand new, squeaky clean housing development, and Tudzhi (Cast Iron), a documentary description of life in an ironworks that singles out individuals on the factory floor not as symbols of thrumming Soviet industrial might, but as human beings.

screenings.title: Falling Leaves
screenings.description: Iosseliani’s debut feature—winner of the FIPRESCI Award at Cannes—follows newly minted oenologists Nico and Otar, just out of winemaking school, as they head to work at an agricultural cooperative in Tbilisi, there to have their first intimate experiences of the opposite sex… as well as their introduction to the corruption bred by stifling bureaucracy and arbitrarily imposed production quotas. A stinging satire of Soviet-style economic planning and its unintended consequences smuggled within a pseudo-documentary depiction of the Georgian wine industry, and a deeply personal film about youth for the first time facing up to the full measure of adult negligence and corruption.

screenings.title: Paranoid Park
screenings.description: Adapting Blake Nelson’s Y.A. novel of the same name, Van Sant renders the youth gathering place of the skate park a voluptuous dreamscape with the help of cinematographers Chris Doyle and Rain Kathy Li. Teenaged skate rat Alex—Gabe Nevins, leading a largely amateur cast recruited via MySpace—finds himself a prime suspect in the death of a security guard, silently carrying a crushing burden of knowledge through his daily rounds, a contrast to the gravity-defying liberation he finds carving it up at “Paranoid Park.”

screenings.title: There Once Was a Singing Blackbird
screenings.description: Gia (Gela Kandelaki), a timpanist in the Tbilisi Philharmonic, has made a science of getting to work just on time to hit his lone cue and then dashing out the door, so as to leave the rest of his hours open for sweet-talking women and carousing with pals. A marvelous character study of an open-handed, incurably impulsive young man infected by the bustling, on-the-go energy of the city around him, and a film that careens along with the same freewheeling spontaneity displayed by its protagonist. Screens with Georgian Ancient Songs, which Iosseliani described thusly: “It’s a film about Georgian traditional polyphony. Georgian songs are always sung in one, two, three or even four voices. It’s a story about how these songs are structured. And at the same time we show what life was like in the old days. The official reaction to the film was one of indignation. I managed to steal a print of the film and keep it safe.”

screenings.title: The Milk of Sorrow
screenings.description: Winner of the Golden Bear at the 59th Berlin International Film Festival, Llosa’s formidable sophomore feature focuses on Fausta (Magaly Solier, in a performance nearly free of dialogue), the only daughter of an aged Indigenous Peruvian woman who, following her mother’s death, must negotiate arrangements for her burial as well as negotiate the smothering legacy of trauma that her parent, horribly misused during the Shining Path terrorist insurgencies of the 1980s and ’90s, has left behind with her child even after herself departing this mortal coil. “Littered with unforgettable images of incongruity, destruction, and, finally, healing” [The Village Voice], The Milk of Sorrow is an exquisitely shot study in inherited injury guarded like a precious heirloom, a work of tragic magic realism.
